questions.question: In a one-to-one mapping between Traveller and Passport, which side owns the link?
options: The side that has the foreign key column and @JoinColumn
The side that has mappedBy
The side with the longer class name
Both sides own it equally
questions.explanation: The owning side stores the foreign key. The inverse side uses mappedBy and only mirrors the link.

questions.question: What does cascade = CascadeType.ALL on the Traveller's passport field do?
options: It makes the passport read-only
It creates a second foreign key
It makes the passport lazy
It passes save and delete from the traveller to the passport
questions.explanation: Cascade carries operations such as persist and remove from the owner to the related entity.

questions.question: Passport 1 already belongs to a traveller. A second traveller is saved pointing at passport 1, and the foreign key column is unique. What happens?
options: Both travellers share the passport
The first traveller is replaced silently
The database rejects the insert with a data-integrity error
The passport is copied with a new id
questions.explanation: A one-to-one foreign key is unique, so a second row cannot point at the same passport.

questions.question: A developer sets passport.setHolder(traveller) but never sets traveller.passport, then saves. What is stored?
options: The link is stored from the inverse side
Nothing links them, because only the owning side writes the foreign key
Both rows are deleted
The passport is saved twice
questions.explanation: Changes made only on the mappedBy side are ignored, so the owning field must be set.

questions.question: Both Traveller and Passport declare @OneToOne with @JoinColumn and no mappedBy. What is the result?
options: Two separate foreign key columns are created, one in each table
Hibernate merges them into one column
The app refuses to compile
One table is dropped
questions.explanation: Without mappedBy each side owns its own link, so the design becomes two independent relationships.
